name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,368

entries.clue: Somewhat before all, I fear for actual human existence (4,4)

indicators.note: 'Somewhat' means a part and not the whole, so only a stretch of the words that follow is taken.

blocks.note: an unbroken run of letters beginning two into 'before' and stopping two into 'fear'

annotation.surface: A nervous speaker owning up: in front of everybody, they are frightened.
annotation.walkthrough: Word breaks and commas are invisible to a buried answer; this run crosses three of them. 'Fear' gives up only its opening FE, which is why the join reads as ordinary punctuation.
annotation.definitionFit: Real life is the ordinary world people actually live in, the thing set against fiction, theory or a screen.

entries.clue: Fail to meet expectations in car venue: hide abroad (12)

indicators.note: 'Abroad' means away from home and scattered about, so the letters are no longer where they belong.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: Someone going to ground overseas, stashed out of sight in a car park.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction and is only a link word — nothing goes inside anything here. The fodder is the whole of 'car venue hide', twelve letters for a twelve-letter light.
annotation.definitionFit: To underachieve is to perform below what your ability promised, which is exactly falling short of what was expected.

entries.clue: One with liability at first demanding extremely broad terms of reference (6)

indicators.note: 'At first' points to the opening of a word, so only the leading letter of each word named is taken.

blocks.clueFragment: demanding extremely broad terms of reference
blocks.note: initials of Demanding Extremely Broad Terms Of Reference

annotation.surface: A negotiator insisting on the widest possible brief before agreeing to start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' usually orders you to take a word's outer letters; here it is just another word donating its initial. Six words follow the instruction and the light is six letters long.
annotation.definitionFit: A debtor is the person who owes the money, so the liability sits on their side of the ledger.

entries.clue: A church feature, high, or long? (6)

blocks.note: the clue's own opening 'A' is the first letter
the spire is the high feature of a church

annotation.surface: A question about church architecture: is the feature a tall one or a long one?
annotation.walkthrough: 'A' reads as an article and is really a letter of the answer — setters lean on that because 'a' vanishes into any surface. The question mark warns that 'long' is wanted as a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To aspire is to yearn and reach for something, which is what 'long' means when it is a verb rather than a measurement.

entries.clue: Ricochet reduced line darts players must stay behind (4)

definitions.text: line darts players must stay behind

indicators.note: 'Reduced' means cut down to less than the whole, so what is left is a shorter run inside the word given.

blocks.note: an unbroken run of four letters starting at the third letter of this word

annotation.surface: A dart bouncing off the wire and skidding back across the throwing line.
annotation.walkthrough: The oche is the raised strip on the floor of a darts match that a thrower's foot must not cross. It is said 'ockey', which is why it looks so unfamiliar written down.
annotation.definitionFit: The oche is precisely that throwing line — the marked limit a darts player has to stay behind.

entries.clue: Meeting Irishman before church (6)

indicators.note: 'Before' fixes the order of the two pieces: what comes before the church goes in front of it.

blocks.note: Sean is the crossword's standard Irish forename
CE = Church of England

annotation.surface: An Irishman turning up at the church ahead of everyone else.
annotation.walkthrough: CE for the Church of England is worth owning outright; setters write plain 'church' for it without further signal. Sean is their default Irishman, alongside Pat and Erin.
annotation.definitionFit: A seance is a sitting — a group gathered round a table for a session — so 'meeting' covers it plainly.

entries.clue: Mark, 100, ultimately superlative — hard to get (6)

indicators.note: 'Ultimately' means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word it governs is taken.

blocks.note: a scar is the mark a wound leaves
C is the Roman hundred
the last letter of superlativE

annotation.surface: A report on an exam: a mark of 100, the best there is, and rarely achieved.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' leads the word it governs instead of trailing it, which is unusual enough to read past. Roman numerals are standing crossword currency: C a hundred, D five hundred, M a thousand.
annotation.definitionFit: Something scarce is in short supply, and the definition names the consequence of that shortage rather than the shortage itself.

entries.clue: Old-fashioned aunt, idle, vain, unfortunately (12)

indicators.note: 'Unfortunately' marks things going wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are no longer in their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A brisk and unkind summary of a relative: lazy, self-regarding and behind the times.
annotation.walkthrough: Adverbs ending in -ly are the commonest hiding place for an anagram signal, because they pass as ordinary comment. The list of insults reads as a sentence and is really a bag of twelve letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Antediluvian means from before Noah's flood, and is used of anything hopelessly out of date — old-fashioned at full strength.

entries.clue: Escape group of ships? Not entirely (4)

indicators.note: 'Not entirely' means short of the whole, so the word is written out with its last letter missing.

blocks.note: FLEET, a group of ships, taken not entirely: the final T is dropped

annotation.surface: A getaway from a flotilla that only half comes off.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'group of ships' as a loose gesture rather than a definition, which is the setter admitting the phrase is there for its letters. Both halves of the clue mean leaving in a hurry.
annotation.definitionFit: To flee is to run away from danger, the plainest word there is for making an escape.

entries.clue: A number sorted tent hire (8)

indicators.note: 'Sorted' is a rearranging word: things put into a new arrangement no longer stand in the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A festival organiser reporting that the renting of the tents has been dealt with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sorted' reads as 'seen to' in the surface and as 'reordered' in the wordplay. 'A number' names only the category, so the fodder does every bit of the deciding.
annotation.definitionFit: Thirteen is a number, and naming the class rather than the value is fair because the anagram fixes which number is meant.

entries.clue: Democrat is eager for changing conflict (8)

indicators.note: 'Changing' means turning into something else, and letters that change places spell something else.

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for a Democrat
IS EAGER shuffled, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A Democrat itching for a war whose shape keeps shifting.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder runs to only seven letters; the eighth comes from 'Democrat', wanted as a party initial rather than as a person. 'Conflict' is the verb here — the sense in which two accounts conflict.
annotation.definitionFit: To disagree is to be at odds with somebody, which is what two people or two reports do when they conflict.

entries.clue: Envied on regular basis period before festival (3)

indicators.note: Doing something on a regular basis is doing it at fixed intervals, so letters are picked at a fixed step through the word.

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of EnViEd

annotation.surface: A person envied at steady intervals during the run-up to a celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regular' most often points at the even letters; here it is the odd ones, and only counting settles which. Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve are the everyday proof of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An eve is the day or evening immediately before a feast day, as in Christmas Eve or All Hallows' Eve.

entries.clue: Urgent order to abandon court (4)

indicators.note: 'To abandon' is to walk away and leave something behind, so the letters named drop out.

blocks.note: DIRECT, meaning to order, abandons CT for court

annotation.surface: A judge telling somebody to get out of the courtroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Court abbreviates to CT the way it does on a street sign, and those two letters happen to sit at the end of the word meaning 'order'. The surface makes both words courtroom words, so the eviction reads as sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dire is desperate and pressing: a dire need is one that will not wait, which is urgency.

entries.clue: Store, maybe, source of verbal accounts? (8)

definitions.note: A store is one kind of the thing rather than the whole class, and 'maybe' is the setter's flag that the definition is by example.

indicators.note: 'Maybe' warns that what stands beside it is only one instance of the answer, not a synonym for it.

blocks.note: first definition: a shop is one of these
second definition: to retail a tale is to pass it on by mouth

annotation.surface: A shop described as the place where all the local gossip starts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retail' carries an older second sense: to retail a story is to repeat it around, which makes the teller one of these. 'Accounts' pulls hard towards shop bookkeeping and means stories.
annotation.definitionFit: A retailer sells to the public, so a store is one; and to retail a tale is to recount it, making a retailer a source of spoken accounts.

entries.clue: Confusion mostly hard to co-ordinate (4)

indicators.note: 'Mostly' means all but a little of a thing, so the word arrives without its final letter.

blocks.note: MESS, meaning confusion, mostly: the last S is left off
H is the pencil grade for hard

annotation.surface: A muddle that is difficult to bring into any kind of order.
annotation.walkthrough: H for hard comes off the side of a pencil, the same convention that gives B for black. The surface reads 'mostly hard' as one phrase, hiding the fact that 'mostly' belongs to the word in front of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Gears mesh when their teeth fit together, and plans mesh when they are co-ordinated so that each one fits the next.

entries.clue: Determined loser coming back, urging tremendous effort initially (8)

indicators.note: 'Coming back' is movement towards where you started, so the letters are read in the opposite direction.
'Initially' means at the outset, so only the opening letter of each word it governs is taken.

blocks.note: LOSER written backwards
the initials of Urging Tremendous Effort

annotation.surface: A beaten player walking back into the fight, spurred on to try enormously hard.
annotation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'coming back' means right to left; the same words in a down clue would mean bottom to top. 'Initially' trails the three words it governs instead of leading them.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody resolute has fixed on a course and will not be shifted from it, which is what being determined amounts to.

entries.clue: To some degree, despicable person, the woman (6)

blocks.note: a rat is a treacherous, despicable person
'her' stands in for the woman

annotation.surface: A grudging verdict on a woman: somewhat of a nasty piece of work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To some degree' looks like a hedge softening the insult and is in fact the whole definition. Pronouns are stock charade material — 'the woman' is HER or SHE, 'the man' HIM or HE.
annotation.definitionFit: Rather means to a moderate extent: 'rather good' is good to some degree but not wholly.

entries.clue: Trim wood (6)

blocks.note: first definition: neat and smart in appearance
second definition: an evergreen conifer and the timber it yields

annotation.surface: A carpenter cutting a length of timber down to size.
annotation.walkthrough: Two-word clues are almost always two definitions, and the shorter the clue the safer that bet. 'Trim' is wanted as an adjective meaning neat, not as the verb the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Spruce means neat and well turned out, as in 'spruce up'; it is also a common evergreen conifer, so 'wood' names both the tree and its timber.

entries.clue: One opposing aim — nothing right! (8)

blocks.note: an object is an aim or purpose
O is nothing, the zero
R is the standard abbreviation for right

annotation.surface: A flat dismissal of somebody's plan: there is nothing right about the aim at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Object' is an aim in the sense of 'the object of the exercise', and it also means to oppose, so the first piece quietly echoes the definition. O for nothing and R for right are among the busiest single letters in the craft.
annotation.definitionFit: An objector is the person who raises the objection, so the definition names them by the thing they do.

entries.clue: Dance sphere (4)

blocks.note: first definition: a formal dancing party
second definition: any perfectly round object

annotation.surface: The world of dance, spoken of as a field with borders of its own.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'dance sphere' sounds like a field of activity; the two words are separate definitions with nothing joining them. The dancing sense and the round one are unrelated in origin, which is why each can be clued straight.
annotation.definitionFit: A ball is a formal dance, the kind with an orchestra and a dress code, and it is also any sphere, from a football to a ball of wool.

entries.clue: Twisted evil mask (4)

indicators.note: Something twisted has been wrenched out of its proper shape, and letters wrenched about no longer read as they did.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: A grotesque carnival mask contorted into a wicked expression.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mask' works as a verb as well as a noun, so the definition stays ambiguous until a crossing settles it. Four-letter anagrams slip past because the fodder looks like an ordinary adjective doing surface work.
annotation.definitionFit: A veil is hung over a face so it cannot be seen, which is the concealing job a mask does.

entries.clue: Claim everything, say, aggressive at the end (6)

indicators.note: 'At the end' names the final position, so the closing letter of the word beside it is the one taken.

blocks.note: everything is all
'say' introduces an example, and eg is the abbreviation for that
the last letter of aggressivE

annotation.surface: An account of a man who demanded the lot and turned nasty by the finish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is one of the busiest words in cryptics: it can mean EG, flag a homophone, or stand for a spoken remark. Here it is the two-letter abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: To allege is to assert something that has not yet been proved, which is what making a claim means.

entries.clue: Drink cartel out of order (6)

indicators.note: Something out of order is not standing in its proper sequence, so the letters are resequenced.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: A price-fixing ring accused of behaving badly over the drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' carries its British sense of misbehaving in the surface and its literal sense in the wordplay. The drink wanted is the British name for red Bordeaux, used here as a plain word for red wine.
annotation.definitionFit: Claret is red Bordeaux, and in Britain the word does duty for red wine generally — a drink.
